analysis|04-12|1961|Ο Γιούρι Γκαγκάριν γίνεται ο πρώτος άνθρωπος στο διάστημα|Yuri Gagarin Becomes the First Human in Space|In the early 1960s the Soviet Union and the United States competed intensely in space technology, after the launch of Sputnik in 1957. The race had military and political dimensions, and every success seemed to prove the superiority of one system over the other. Astronauts had not yet travelled into space. // On 12 April 1961 the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin completed one orbit around the Earth in the spacecraft Vostok 1, on a flight that lasted about 108 minutes. It was the first time a human being had reached orbit. The achievement caused worldwide enthusiasm and a strong reaction in the United States. // Gagarin's flight gave the Soviet Union a leading advantage in the space rivalry. The American reaction led to an acceleration of space research and to large investments in science, and this development pushed the United States to strengthen NASA, which had been founded in 1958, and to set the goal of landing on the Moon. The flight had an international impact and strengthened the Soviet image. The American success came a few years later with the landing. The moment remains in history as a milestone of human exploration.

analysis|04-12|1981|Πρώτη πτήση του διαστημικού λεωφορείου|First Flight of the Space Shuttle|In the early 1980s NASA had developed the space shuttle, a reusable spacecraft that was expected to reduce the cost of missions. The programme had great expectations, but also many technical challenges. Tests had progressed and a date had been set for the first flight. // On 12 April 1981 the space shuttle Columbia was launched from Cape Canaveral in Florida. This flight was the first of its kind with a crew, and it marked the beginning of a new era in space transport. The launch took place exactly twenty years after Gagarin's flight. // Columbia completed its first mission, and hundreds of flights of the shuttle programme followed. The programme proved valuable for research, but also tragic, with the losses of the Challenger and the Columbia. Reusability of the vehicles was expected to reduce the cost of spaceflight, although in practice the cost proved high. The shuttle programme contributed to important missions, such as the servicing of the Hubble telescope. The evolution of the programme remains as one of the most ambitious efforts of its time. Its history remains an important chapter in space technology.

analysis|04-13|1743|Γεννιέται ο Τόμας Τζέφερσον|Thomas Jefferson Is Born|In the eighteenth century Virginia was one of the richest British colonies of North America, with an economy based on plantations and slavery. The educated families of the colonists had been influenced by the ideas of the Enlightenment, and the debate on the autonomy of the colonies was growing. The education of young men from the upper classes was often private. // On 13 April 1743 Thomas Jefferson was born at Shadwell in Virginia, into a planter family. Jefferson studied law and politics, and quickly became known for his intellectual activity. His early engagement with the political questions of the colonial period led him to a great deal of active involvement. // Jefferson became the author of the Declaration of Independence of 1776 and later the third president of the United States, from 1801 to 1809. The declaration set out the principles of natural rights as the basis of the state, at the same time as he himself owned slaves. Jefferson was a learned polymath with interests in architecture, agriculture and education, and he founded the University of Virginia. Jefferson also took an interest in architecture and cultivation, and his versatility ties his name to the Enlightenment.

analysis|04-13|1970|Το ατύχημα του Απόλλων 13|The Apollo 13 accident|Within the space age, the Apollo 13 mission aimed to land on the Moon, in an area called Fra Mauro. The spacecraft consisted of the command module and the service module, which provided power, oxygen and propulsion. The astronauts had already begun the journey to the Moon. // On 13 April 1970 an oxygen tank exploded in the service module, which forced the crew to move into the command module. Power and oxygen fell sharply, and the landing was cancelled. The astronauts and the mission control centre in Houston worked together to find a way to return. // The crew returned safely to Earth on 17 April, after a return that is regarded as one of the greatest successes of crisis management in the space age. Engineers in the control centre worked with the crew to save power, water and oxygen. The incident led to significant technical changes in spacecraft, with consequences for later missions. The choice of a trajectory that made use of the Moon's gravity was decisive for the success. The incident also became known as a symbol of crisis in public discussion. The astronauts remain in history as an example of composure.

analysis|04-13|1970|Η έκρηξη στον Απόλλωνα 13|The Explosion on Apollo 13|Within the space age, the Apollo 13 mission aimed to land on the Moon, in an area called Fra Mauro. The spacecraft consisted of the command module and the service module, which provided power, oxygen and propulsion. Power and oxygen fell sharply, and the landing was cancelled. The choice of a trajectory that made use of the Moon's gravity was decisive for the success. The incident also became known as a symbol of crisis in public discussion. The astronauts remain in history as an example of composure.

analysis|04-14|1205|Η μάχη της Αδριανούπολης|The Battle of Adrianople|In the early thirteenth century Constantinople had been captured by the crusaders of the Fourth Crusade in 1204, and the Latin Empire was established. Bulgaria, led by Kaloyan, was emerging as a strong power in the Balkans and was competing with the new rulers of the region. The Latins were politically and militarily weak in the countryside. // In 1205 Kaloyan defeated the Latin forces near Adrianople, on 14 April. In this battle Emperor Baldwin I was captured, and he died later in captivity. The victory considerably strengthened the Bulgarian position and revealed the vulnerability of the Latin Empire. // This defeat weakened the Latin Empire, which was unable to regain its lost positions. Kaloyan's victory strengthened Bulgarian power and limited the plans of the crusaders in the wider region. Bulgaria appeared as an important factor in the Balkans. The Latin defeat forced the crusaders to reconsider their strategy in the Balkans. The rise of Bulgaria would for years be a key factor in the region. The period was connected with new balances in Byzantine history. The history of the clash is studied as part of Balkan history. This particular clash is a central point of the Byzantine period.

analysis|04-14|1849|Η Ουγγαρία διακηρύσσει την ανεξαρτησία της|Hungary declares its independence|At the outbreak of the revolution of 1848 in Europe, Hungary was claiming autonomy from the Habsburgs. The Hungarian leaders, headed by Lajos Kossuth, demanded political rights and an independent government. The clash with the imperial administration had developed into a war. // On 14 April 1849 the Hungarian parliament declared the independence of the country and the removal of the Habsburg dynasty. Kossuth took over the government as governor. The declaration showed the determination of the Hungarians, although the military situation was already precarious. // The revolution was ultimately met with Russian and Austrian military intervention, and independence was crushed. The leaders of the movement were convicted or exiled, and Hungary remained under Austrian control for years. Autonomy was restored later with the Compromise of 1867. Historians point out that the independence of 1849 was brief, but it left deep marks on the national consciousness of the Hungarians. The process that led to the Compromise of 1867 gave Hungary autonomy within Austria-Hungary. The uprising influenced the international debate on the national rights of peoples. Kossuth became a symbol of Hungarian national memory. The reforms of the period left a long-term imprint. The revolution remains a central chapter of Hungarian history.

analysis|04-14|1865|Πυροβολείται ο Αβραάμ Λίνκολν|Abraham Lincoln Is Shot|In early 1865 the American Civil War was nearing its end, and President Abraham Lincoln had begun a second term. The Union had won significant victories, while the Confederacy was facing exhaustion. The political debate on peace and the reunification of the nation was at the centre of national life. // On 14 April 1865 John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in Washington, where the president was watching a performance. Lincoln was carried to a nearby house and died the next day, 15 April. The murder took place as part of a conspiracy that also aimed at other government officials. // Lincoln's death shocked the country and left Reconstruction in the hands of Andrew Johnson. The policy of the following years determined the relations of the states with the federation and the fate of the freed slaves. Lincoln had led the country through the difficult period of the civil war, and his murder took place a few days after Lee's surrender. Booth's conspiracy led to trials and strict security measures. Booth was killed a few weeks later. The murder marked a turning point in the politics of Reconstruction. The day of his death remains a day of memory in national history.

analysis|04-14|1912|Ο Τιτανικός χτυπά σε παγόβουνο|The Titanic Strikes an Iceberg|In the early twentieth century the ocean liner Titanic was sailing in the North Atlantic, despite warnings of the presence of icebergs in the area. Navigation at that time relied on radio telegraphy and observation, and crews had limited means of recognising ice. The speed of the ship remained high, despite the conditions. // Shortly before midnight on 14 April 1912 the ship struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. The damage opened several compartments at the bow, and the inflow of water was uncontrollable. The lifeboats were not enough for all the passengers and crew. // The disaster left about 1,500 dead, and its scale provoked international debate on safety rules at sea. The international convention for the safety of life at sea was revised after the event. The lack of sufficient lifeboats and the slow reaction of the crews increased the losses, while the collision was not recognised in time as serious. The case was examined in British and American inquiries. The assessment of responsibilities contributed to the development of navigation regulations. The survivors described the events of that night in detail. The tragedy is still studied as a case for teaching. The event remains in memory as a symbol of the helplessness of technology before nature.

analysis|04-14|1931|Η Δεύτερη Ισπανική Δημοκρατία|The Second Spanish Republic|In early 1931 Spain was in a deep political and economic crisis. The dictatorship of Primo de Rivera had collapsed in 1930, and confidence in the monarchy had weakened considerably. The global economic crisis had worsened unemployment and rural poverty, while demands for reform had intensified. // On 12 April 1931 municipal elections were held, which gave a clear victory to the republicans in the big cities. The government could not ignore the result, and King Alfonso XIII decided to leave the country. On 14 April 1931 the Second Spanish Republic was proclaimed, with a peaceful transition. // The new republic promoted reforms, such as in education, women's right to vote and the separation of church and state. Tensions, however, increased, and in 1936 a civil war broke out that lasted until 1939. The Second Republic remains in history as a period of great political confrontation and at the same time of significant reforms. The dictatorship and the economic crisis had caused discontent in many social strata. The transition was relatively peaceful and was accepted by a large part of society. The reforms of the republic provoked reactions from conservative circles.

analysis|04-15|1755|Εκδίδεται το Λεξικό του Τζόνσον|Johnson's Dictionary Is Published|In the mid-eighteenth century the English language did not have a single and reliable dictionary, and spelling and the meaning of words varied from place to place. Scholars and publishers sought a standard work that would define the correct use of the language. Earlier dictionaries were small or limited. // On 15 April 1755 Samuel Johnson published the dictionary of the English language, an extensive work that he had compiled almost alone over a long period. The dictionary included definitions, examples from literature and etymological notes. Johnson had begun the work several years earlier, with the support of publishers. // The dictionary became the main reference work of the English language for about a century. With his work Johnson shaped the understanding of correct word usage and spelling. The need for a reliable dictionary was linked with the spread of education and printing. The need for a reliable dictionary was linked with the spread of education and printing. The work gave a firm foundation to the use of the language. Johnson was a writer of great influence on the letters of his age.

analysis|04-15|1912|Βυθίζεται ο Τιτανικός|The Titanic Sinks|In the early twentieth century navigation in the North Atlantic was intense, with ocean liners carrying passengers and goods between Europe and America. Competition between companies resulted in ever larger and faster ships, which followed the usual routes. The movement of ice at sea was well known, but it did not always have strong preventive measures. // The Titanic sank on 15 April 1912, a few minutes after two in the morning, on her maiden voyage to New York. Thousands of passengers and crew members found themselves in the sea, in freezing conditions. The ship Carpathia arrived later and picked up the survivors. // The tragedy, with more than 1,500 dead, provoked worldwide grief and led to stricter safety rules, such as more lifeboats and international monitoring of ice. That disaster led to international conventions on the safety of navigation. The story of the Titanic is still taught as an example of the need for humility before nature. That disaster led to international conventions on the safety of navigation. Continuous monitoring of ice and lifeboats became compulsory. The story of the Titanic is still taught as an example of the need for humility.

analysis|04-15|1989|Πεθαίνει ο Χου Γιαοπάνγκ|Hu Yaobang Dies|In the late 1980s China was in a phase of economic reforms, which had opened the country to markets but had also brought social tensions. Inflation, corruption and restrictions on freedom of expression caused discontent, particularly among students in the cities. Hu Yaobang, general secretary of the Communist Party, was regarded as a supporter of the reforms and had already faced political difficulties. // On 15 April 1989 Hu Yaobang died, and his death became the occasion for student gatherings in Tiananmen Square in Beijing. The demonstrations quickly grew, with demands for transparency, freedom of the press and dialogue with the leadership. Over the following weeks the gatherings spread to many cities in the country. // The government responded by declaring martial law and, in the early hours of 4 June, by sending the army into the square. The number of dead remains a matter of dispute, with estimates varying widely. The event remains in history as a symbol of the suppression of protest, and the Chinese leadership has avoided discussing it openly within the country. That situation left deep marks on the political life of the country. The event is regarded as a turning point for the modern history of the country and for the debate on human rights.

analysis|04-16|1853|Λειτουργεί η πρώτη σιδηροδρομική γραμμή της Ινδίας|India's First Railway Line Opens|In the early nineteenth century India was under British rule through the East India Company, and Britain sought to develop infrastructure that would facilitate trade and administration. Transport by cart and ship was slow, and the need for a railway was ever more urgent. Investment came from private companies with British capital and guarantees. // On 16 April 1853 the first train service in India began, from Bombay to Thane, over a distance of about 34 kilometres. The train carried passengers and goods, and the news aroused great interest in local society. This line is regarded as the starting point of Indian railways. // In the following years the network expanded across the country, and the railway became the basic infrastructure for transporting troops, products and people. This development contributed to the economic integration of India, but it served primarily the interests of the colonial administration. The railway remains today one of the most important public networks in the country. This line was short in length, but it opened the way to the wider development of the Indian network. Its success showed colonial officials that investment in railways could bring results. Investments multiplied in the years that followed.

analysis|04-16|1912|Η Χάριετ Κουίμπι πετά πάνω από τη Μάγχη|Harriet Quimby Flies Across the English Channel|In the early twentieth century aviation was still a pioneering field, with pilots testing the limits of aircraft and their endurance. Crossing the English Channel by aeroplane was one of the great challenges, as the distance was relatively short but the sea was dangerous for the light aircraft of the period. Women pilots were very few, and each of their achievements was important for social acceptance. // On 16 April 1912 the American pilot Harriet Quimby crossed the Channel in a single-engined aeroplane, and became the first woman to do so. The flight was made from France to England, in cold and windy conditions. Her success brought great publicity to aviation. // Quimby's flight opened the way for other women pilots and showed that aviation could be a field of action for women. She herself lost her life a few months later in an air accident, and her memory remains as a symbol of boldness at the dawn of the aviation age. Her flight is regarded as one of the most important achievements of early aviation. Quimby's flight inspired other women pilots and helped to challenge social prejudices about aviation.

analysis|04-16|1945|Αρχίζει η μάχη του Βερολίνου|The Battle of Berlin Begins|In early 1945 the Second World War was nearing its end, and the Red Army had advanced deep into Germany. Eastern Europe had been liberated from German troops, while Berlin was the capital of the Nazi regime and the final target of the Soviet offensive. Negotiations on the postwar order had already begun in the shadow of the conflict. // On 16 April 1945 the Soviet offensive on Berlin began, with massive forces of infantry, armour and artillery. The battle was among the hardest of the war in Europe, with fighting in the city streets and heavy bombardment. German resistance was fierce, but the balance of forces became ever less favourable for the defenders. // The Battle of Berlin ended with the surrender of the capital in early May, and the war in Europe ended a few days later. Losses, for civilians and soldiers alike, were enormous, and much of the city was destroyed. The event determined the postwar division of Germany and the position of Berlin in the Cold War. This battle is one of the critical points of the final phase of the war in Europe. This battle was harsh for civilians, who lived among the ruins of the city for weeks.

analysis|04-17|1492|Συμφωνία των Καθολικών Μοναρχών με τον Κολόμβο|Agreement of the Catholic Monarchs with Columbus|At the end of the fifteenth century Spain was being unified under the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, and the war with the emirate of Granada was coming to an end. The monarchs were seeking new trade routes to the East and wanted to strengthen their authority abroad. Columbus had proposed a voyage to the west, but he needed funding and political support. // On 17 April 1492 the Capitulations of Santa Fe were signed, which set out the rights and obligations of the two sides. The monarchs undertook to finance the voyage, while Columbus would receive titles, a share of the profits and rights of administration over the new lands. That agreement opened the way for the first expedition. // The agreement changed the course of European history, because the voyages that followed brought America into the European sphere. These agreements were the starting point of a long colonial period, with deep consequences for the peoples of America and for world trade. This treaty is regarded today as one of the basic texts of the age of the great discoveries. These agreements contained detailed terms on shares, titles and rights of future colonies, and they were the subject of strict debate in the court of the monarchs.

analysis|04-17|1946|Η Συρία αποκτά την ανεξαρτησία της|Syria gains its independence|In the mid-twentieth century Syria was under French mandate rule, which had been established after the First World War. The nationalist movement had developed strongly, and demonstrations against the French presence had increased. France had formally recognised gradual independence, but in practice it was delayed. Syrian leaders pressed for the complete withdrawal of the troops. // On 17 April 1946 the last French troops left, and Syria became fully independent. That day was established as a national holiday and marked the end of French presence in the country. The transition came after negotiations and pressure from the Syrians themselves. // Independence opened a period of political instability, with coups and changes of regime in the following decades. The country became a member of the United Nations and an important factor in the Middle East. This history is connected with the disputes over national identity and sovereignty in the region. Syria's independence, however, also brought internal tensions between political groups, which made it difficult to organise the state. The French presence had left administrative structures that had to be adapted to the new needs. The negotiations with France had lasted and had many stages, and final independence was the result of continuous pressure from the national movement.

analysis|04-17|1961|Η απόβαση στον Κόλπο των Χοίρων|The Bay of Pigs Invasion|In the early 1960s the United States government was concerned about the government of Fidel Castro in Cuba, which had aligned itself with the Soviet Union. The CIA had developed a plan to overthrow it with Cuban exiles, and President Kennedy had agreed to its implementation. The operation had been designed as a rapid landing that would provoke an uprising on the island. // On 17 April 1961 hundreds of exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs, but Cuban forces reacted quickly. The operation did not receive the expected support from the population, and the invaders were captured within a few days. The failure was public and humiliating for the United States. // The incident intensified Cuba's opposition to the United States and led the Cuban government to turn even more towards the Soviet Union. The operation became a lesson for American intelligence services and contributed to the missile crisis of the following year. The Bay of Pigs remains a point of reference in relations between the United States and Cuba. The failure of the operation also affected the international image of the United States, since their involvement was widely seen as obvious. The confrontation remained in memory as a lesson about American intelligence services and the limits of covert operations.

analysis|04-17|1975|Οι Ερυθροί Χμερ καταλαμβάνουν την Πνομ Πενχ|The Khmer Rouge Take Phnom Penh|In the early 1970s Cambodia was in a civil war, and the country had been drawn into the conflict of Vietnam. The Khmer Rouge, a communist movement led by Pol Pot, were developing from the rural areas and their forces were constantly growing. The government of Lon Nol, which had been overthrown in 1970, could not withstand the pressure. // On 17 April 1975 the Khmer Rouge entered Phnom Penh, the capital, and the population was violently evacuated to the countryside. Hospitals, schools and public services were dissolved, and the city was emptied within a few days. The evacuation marked the beginning of a period of extreme repression. // The rule of the Khmer Rouge led to mass deaths from starvation, exhaustion, executions and forced labour, with estimates reaching one to two million dead. The regime was overthrown in 1979 by Vietnamese intervention, and this period is a central chapter in the history of Cambodia and of international law. This conflict left deep marks on the society of the country. The news of the capture of the capital caused fear and confusion, while many inhabitants left their homes within a few hours.

analysis|04-18|1906|Ο μεγάλος σεισμός του Σαν Φρανσίσκο|The Great San Francisco Earthquake|In the early twentieth century America was developing rapidly, and San Francisco was one of the most important ports of the West, with fast economic growth and a large population increase. The city had been built on an area with active faults, and the buildings of the period were largely wooden or of weak construction. The seismic activity of the area was known, but protective measures were limited. // On 18 April 1906 a powerful earthquake struck the north-western part of the state of California, and fires followed that destroyed most of the buildings in the centre. The thousands of inhabitants left homeless tried to find shelter in parks and in temporary camps. The fires lasted several days and destroyed records and infrastructure. // The disaster led to extensive reconstruction, to new building rules and to important studies of earthquakes in the area. The city was rebuilt in a short time, and the event remains part of the memory of California and of seismology. The area continues to be regarded as seismically active. This disaster changed the understanding of city planning in earthquake-prone regions, and urban administration began to apply stricter building codes.

analysis|04-18|1942|Η επιδρομή Ντουλίτλ|The Doolittle Raid|In early 1942, after the attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States was seeking ways to show that it could respond to Japan and to strengthen the morale of the people. Japan had won significant victories in the Pacific, and the idea of bombing Tokyo was politically and militarily desirable. The operation required particular boldness, since the aircraft had to take off from an aircraft carrier. // On 18 April 1942 a group of American bombers, under the command of James Doolittle, bombed Tokyo and other Japanese cities. The operation had limited military value, but it caused damage and shock in Japanese public opinion. Most of the aircraft could not land at their bases and crashed or landed in China. // The operation strengthened American morale and led Japan to reinforce the defence of its islands. The mission remains in history as one of the boldest air operations of the war. This operation showed that American aviation could reach far beyond its bases. This operation also had a psychological character, since it showed that Japan's military power was not invulnerable. The idea was much discussed within the American staff, and many military leaders considered its success uncertain.

analysis|04-18|1980|Η Ζιμπάμπουε γίνεται ανεξάρτητο κράτος|Zimbabwe Becomes an Independent State|In the early 1980s Rhodesia, a British colony in southern Africa, was engaged in a long war between the white minority that governed it and the African nationalist movements. International pressure had increased, and Britain sought a solution that would lead to independence with majority rule. The agreement reached at Lancaster House provided for elections under British supervision. // On 18 April 1980 the country became an independent state under the name Zimbabwe, and Robert Mugabe was elected as the first prime minister. Independence marked the end of colonial rule by the white minority, and the new leader took over the government with great popular support. The transition took place with the participation of international observers. // Independence opened a period of economic and political difficulties, and later Mugabe established an authoritarian regime that repressed the opposition. The example of the country remains a point of reference in discussions on the transition from colonialism to democracy in Africa. This history became part of the great questions about the independence of African states. The independence of the country also caused extensive debates about the rights of the white community, which influenced the negotiations of the period.

analysis|04-19|1775|Οι μάχες του Λέξινγκτον και του Κόνκορντ|The Battles of Lexington and Concord|In the 1770s the confrontation between Britain and the American colonies had intensified over taxes and restrictions on trade. Colonial militias and British forces exchanged threats, and the weapons in the colonies were gathered in storehouses. Boston, the main centre of resistance, had become the point of great tension. // On 19 April 1775 British troops moved towards Concord to seize weapons of the colonists, and at Lexington they clashed with militiamen. The first shots of the war of independence were heard there, and several people were killed. The British forces continued towards Concord, where the colonial army met them. // This clash led to the siege of Boston and to a wider uprising in the colonies. A few months later the Second Continental Congress convened, and the independence of the colonies became ever more likely. This battle is regarded as the beginning of the American Revolutionary War. This moment remains in American memory as the starting point of national history. The British government considered colonial control necessary, while colonial leaders demanded greater autonomy in their decisions. These tensions had begun to shape the political culture of the colonies, which acquired their own institutions of consultation.

analysis|04-19|1775|Οι πρώτες μάχες του Αμερικανικού Επαναστατικού Πολέμου|The First Battles of the American Revolutionary War|The confrontation between Britain and the American colonies had been in progress for years, with demands for fiscal and political autonomy. British laws and the presence of troops in the cities had provoked strong reaction, and the colonial militias were now on alert. The two sides were waiting for a pretext for conflict. // On 19 April 1775 the pretext came, when British forces clashed with American militiamen at Lexington and fighting followed at Concord in Massachusetts. The British mission aimed to locate and seize stocks of weapons, and the militiamen reacted. The first casualties were militiamen and soldiers on both sides. // These battles opened the way to the war that would lead to the declaration of independence in 1776. This moment remains in American memory as the starting point of national history, and many celebrations are still connected with these events today. These battles are regarded as the first step towards the independence of the United States. This particular clash lasted only a few hours, but its consequences were long-lasting for the colonies. The cause of the clash was not great, but the political tension gave every act a weight that went beyond its local dimension.

analysis|04-19|1943|Η εξέγερση του Γκέτο της Βαρσοβίας|The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising|In early 1943 the Nazi forces had established an occupation regime in Poland, and the Warsaw ghetto was the place where the Jewish population was confined. Mass deportations to extermination camps had already begun, and the inhabitants knew the danger. Resistance groups had been organised in secret, with the few weapons they could obtain. // In April 1943, on the eve of Passover, the Germans attempted to clear the ghetto, and the resistance of the people was unexpected. The fighters of the Jewish Combat Organisation, with limited weapons, fought for weeks. The uprising was suppressed with extensive destruction of the ghetto. // The uprising became the symbol of Jewish resistance to the occupation and of dignity in the face of extermination. Among the ruined cities after the war, the memory of the uprising was established as part of national and international history. The uprising remains one of the most important reference points for resistance during the Holocaust. This resistance was one of the few cases of armed resistance inside a ghetto in all of occupied Europe. The history of the ghetto is studied today as an example of human endurance and of the power of memory.

analysis|04-19|1995|Η βομβιστική επίθεση στην Οκλαχόμα|The Oklahoma City Bombing|In the early 1990s the United States faced growing concern about domestic terrorism, with groups opposed to the government and armed militant organisations. The political debate on gun control and strict security measures was intense. The federal government building in Oklahoma City was one of the symbols of American administration in the area. // On 19 April 1995 a lorry loaded with explosives blew up in front of the Alfred P. Murrah building, and 168 people were killed, among them children who were in the building's day-care centre. The perpetrator, Timothy McVeigh, was arrested, tried and sentenced to death. The attack caused shock across the whole country. // The tragedy led to stricter safety rules for public buildings and to new measures for monitoring domestic terrorism. The memorial in Oklahoma City, opened later, is today a place of memory for the victims and survivors. The attack remains among the most serious domestic terrorist acts in the history of the United States. After the attack the American authorities recognised the need for better coordination between federal and local agencies. The debate on the American role in the security of cities continued for years after the incident.

analysis|04-20|1902|Οι Κιουρί απομονώνουν το ράδιο|The Curies Isolate Radium|At the end of the nineteenth century the science of radioactivity was a new field, and researchers were trying to understand the properties of the new elements. Marie and Pierre Curie had discovered polonium and radium, but isolating them was difficult and expensive. Researchers needed large quantities of minerals and a great deal of time to make progress. // In 1902 the Curies managed to chemically isolate radium from the mineral uranium, after processing large quantities of material over several years. The effort required patience and method, and the results were particularly important for physics. Radium was measured and described with precision. // The discovery contributed to the understanding of radioactivity and opened the way to medical applications of radiation, such as in cancer therapy. The work of the Curies earned them the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, and Marie Curie later received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as well. Their work remains fundamental to modern nuclear science. The work of the Curies required large quantities of uranium, which they processed in a very poor laboratory, with serious risks to their health. Their work was recognised internationally, and it opened the way to new laboratories in Europe and the United States.
